assets.title: How to Map Canopy Light
assets.altText: Canopy PPFD mapping diagram showing a repeatable crop-plane grid, spatial variation, sensor orientation and remapping triggers.
assets.teachingPurpose: Teach learners to preserve the spatial PPFD pattern, keep geometry repeatable, and distinguish useful summary statistics from the underlying map.
expandedScience: A useful light map preserves raw point values rather than only the mean because edge loss, overlap valleys and hot spots can be hidden by an average.
Crop-plane height, sensor orientation, fixture power, canopy height and grid coordinates should remain fixed or documented between maps.
Re-map after changes to fixture height, dimming, spacing, reflective geometry or canopy architecture because each can change distribution.
Minimum, maximum, range and mean help compare maps, but the spatial pattern still matters and two maps with the same mean can distribute light very differently.
PPFD interpretation must remain contextual to crop stage, genetics, carbon dioxide, temperature, water status, nutrition and canopy geometry.

assets.title: Root-Zone Sampling Methods
assets.altText: Comparison of runoff, pour-through, slurry or dilution, and saturated-media extract root-zone sampling methods with method-specific interpretation cautions.
assets.teachingPurpose: Prevent learners from treating method-specific pH and EC values as interchangeable and explain why runoff is not a direct biopsy of the entire rhizosphere.
expandedScience: Runoff, pour-through, slurry or dilution extracts and saturated-media extracts sample different solution fractions and dilution states.
Changing extraction method can change the reported value even when the crop has not materially changed.
Drainage chemistry reflects the flow path through the container, so poorly wetted or bypassed regions may contribute little or nothing to the runoff sample.
Reference ranges must be matched to the sampling method used; method-specific ranges should not be exchanged without explicit validation.
Sample identity, method, timing relative to irrigation, instrument, units, calibration state and temperature handling should remain attached to the result.

assets.title: Trichome Sampling & Microscope Technique
assets.altText: Representative trichome sampling diagram showing multiple flower positions, flower versus sugar-leaf tissue, standardized microscopy and multiple-field interpretation.
assets.teachingPurpose: Teach representative trichome sampling and show why tissue type, canopy position, magnification, illumination and field selection affect harvest interpretation.
expandedScience: One sugar leaf, one flower tip or one microscope field may not represent the maturity of an entire plant or batch.
Trichomes on sugar leaves can mature differently from glandular trichomes on flower bracts, so tissue identity should be recorded.
Maturity can vary by canopy position and flower, making multi-location sampling more informative than a single convenient sample.
Magnification and lighting should be standardized enough that repeat images remain comparable.
Trichome appearance should be interpreted together with whole-plant development, flower condition, cultivar history and repeated observations rather than as a single absolute harvest trigger.
